ego.name: Alexander Hamilton
primary_roles: first U.S. secretary of the treasury
ego.summary: Alexander Hamilton was a Caribbean-born American statesman, Revolutionary War officer, lawyer, and Founding Father. As George Washington's aide-de-camp and later the first U.S. secretary of the treasury, he helped shape the early federal government, financial system, and Federalist Party.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton’s mother, who raised Alexander and his elder brother in the West Indies after their father left the family. Her death from fever in 1768 orphaned him.
shared_activities: Family life in Nevis and Saint Croix
connections.notes: Her estate was seized after her death, though family books were recovered for Hamilton.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's older brother and childhood companion. The brothers were orphaned together after their mother's death but were subsequently separated.
shared_activities: Childhood in Nevis and Saint Croix
Shared private schooling and family library
connections.notes: James Jr. was apprenticed to a carpenter after the brothers were separated.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's Scottish-born father, who lived with Rachel Faucette and their two sons in Nevis before abandoning the family during Alexander's childhood.
shared_activities: Correspondence, including Hamilton's later account of the 1772 hurricane
connections.notes: The exact year of his departure is uncertain; the relationship was substantially disrupted by his abandonment of the household.

connections.relationship_description: Merchant associated with Beekman and Cruger, the Saint Croix import-export firm where teenage Hamilton worked as a clerk and was trusted to manage operations while an owner was absent.
connections.notes: Hamilton's early responsibility in the firm contributed to his later financial and administrative competence.

connections.relationship_description: Presbyterian minister, tutor, and early mentor in Saint Croix who submitted Hamilton's vivid 1772 hurricane letter for publication, helping prompt local patrons to fund his education in North America.
shared_activities: Mobilizing support for Hamilton's educational migration
connections.notes: Knox's intervention was pivotal to Hamilton's departure from Saint Croix.

connections.relationship_description: Irish-born New York merchant and early host who boarded Hamilton when he first arrived in New York, assisted him with educational finances, and remained a Revolutionary-era associate.
shared_activities: Selling cargo to fund Hamilton's education
Hearts of Oak and Sons of Liberty activities
connections.notes: Hamilton again boarded with Mulligan while beginning his studies at King's College.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's King's College roommate, fellow member of an early literary society, and lifelong friend who recalled Hamilton's early public defense of the Patriot cause.
shared_activities: Unnamed literary society preceding the Philolexian Society
Patriot political discussion and Revolutionary-era friendship
connections.notes: Troup's testimony is a key source for Hamilton's early public reputation as a persuasive Patriot speaker.

connections.relationship_description: Loyalist Anglican clergyman and pamphleteer whose writings Hamilton anonymously rebutted in 1774, launching Hamilton's public political-writing career.
shared_activities: Public pamphlet controversy over the Patriot and Loyalist causes
Hamilton's A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress
connections.notes: Their relationship was an adversarial intellectual exchange rather than a personal association.

connections.relationship_description: New York legal and political associate who worked with Hamilton in the Revolutionary movement, constitutional ratification campaign, and Federalist political network.
shared_activities: Federalist Party and national political affairs
connections.notes: Hamilton supported the Jay Treaty as part of his broader pro-British commercial and diplomatic policy.

connections.relationship_description: A fellow Continental Army officer and one of Hamilton's closest Revolutionary War friends. Their surviving correspondence reflects an intense and affectionate friendship, while claims of a sexual relationship remain unsubstantiated.
shared_activities: Correspondence on war, politics, and Laurens's antislavery military proposals
connections.notes: Hamilton mourned Laurens's 1782 death deeply.

connections.relationship_description: Continental Army commander-in-chief who selected Hamilton as an aide-de-camp in 1777 and later appointed him secretary of the treasury. Their relationship combined close professional trust, intermittent tension, and lasting political influence.
shared_activities: Revolutionary War strategy, correspondence, intelligence, and diplomacy
Federal financial system and national-government building
connections.notes: Hamilton left Washington's staff in 1781 seeking field command, but later fought under him at Yorktown.

connections.relationship_description: French-born Continental Army general and a close Revolutionary War correspondent of Hamilton. They worked within Washington’s command network and during the Yorktown campaign.
connections.notes: Hamilton's letters to Lafayette have been read differently by historians; the supplied text does not establish a sexual relationship.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton’s wife, with whom he raised eight children. They reconciled after the Reynolds affair, and after his death she preserved his papers and defended his legacy.
shared_activities: Assistance with Hamilton's political and financial writings
Managing homes in Albany, New York, and Philadelphia
connections.notes: Eliza survived Hamilton by 50 years and worked to preserve his papers and public reputation.

connections.relationship_description: Elizabeth Hamilton's father, Continental Army general, New York political leader, and an important connection to Hamilton's entry into the Schuyler social and political network.
shared_activities: Hamilton's courtship and marriage to Elizabeth at the Schuyler Mansion
Federalist and New York political networks
Family gatherings and shared public life
connections.notes: Hamilton's political support for Federalism aligned closely with his father-in-law's positions; Aaron Burr defeated Schuyler for a Senate seat in 1791.

connections.relationship_description: Elizabeth Hamilton’s mother and matriarch of the Schuyler household, where Hamilton married Eliza and joined a prominent New York family.
shared_activities: Care and support for Elizabeth during wartime and family separations
connections.notes: She died in 1803, shortly before Hamilton's death.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's eldest child, named for Philip Schuyler. His fatal 1801 duel with George Eacker caused profound grief for Hamilton and the family.
shared_activities: Advice before Philip's duel with George Eacker
connections.notes: Philip's death near Weehawken preceded Hamilton's fatal duel at the same general location by less than three years.

connections.relationship_description: Early collaborator in the movement for constitutional reform and co-author of The Federalist Papers, who later became one of Hamilton's principal ideological opponents over finance, federal power, and party politics.
connections.notes: Their cooperation on the Constitution gave way to rivalry as Madison joined Jefferson in organizing opposition to Hamilton's Federalist program.

connections.relationship_description: Federalist president whose handling of the Quasi-War Hamilton criticized. Adams appointed Hamilton major general, but Hamilton later opposed Adams's 1800 reelection.
connections.notes: Hamilton's opposition to Adams contributed to divisions within the Federalist Party.

connections.relationship_description: Secretary of state in Washington's cabinet and leader of the Democratic-Republicans. Jefferson opposed Hamilton's financial program, but Hamilton nevertheless backed Jefferson over Burr in the disputed presidential election of 1800.
shared_activities: Debates over finance, federal authority, and foreign policy
connections.notes: Hamilton regarded Jefferson as a political adversary but considered Burr more dangerous and unprincipled.

connections.relationship_description: New York political rival whose conflict with Hamilton culminated in the 1804 duel at Weehawken. Burr fatally wounded Hamilton after years of electoral, legal, and personal antagonism.
shared_activities: New York legal and political competition
connections.notes: Hamilton's opposition to Burr's election in 1800 and candidacy for New York governor in 1804 intensified their long-running rivalry.

connections.relationship_description: Hamilton's mistress in Philadelphia during 1791–1792. Her husband, James Reynolds, used the affair to extort payments from Hamilton, leading to a major public scandal when Hamilton published the Reynolds Pamphlet in 1797.
connections.notes: Hamilton's public admission of the affair was meant to rebut allegations of financial misconduct in office.

category_summaries.summary: Hamilton's early family life was marked by his parents' nonmarital relationship, his father's departure, and the death of his mother, which left him orphaned. His later marriage to Elizabeth Schuyler integrated him into the influential Schuyler family and provided a lasting household and intellectual partnership.

Hamilton's professional network joined military patronage, constitutional collaboration, financial administration, and sharp party conflict. Washington was the central patron and collaborator, while Madison, Jefferson, Adams, Burr, and others became consequential allies or adversaries in the politics of the early republic.

Hamilton's personal network included formative hosts and lifelong friends such as Hercules Mulligan, Robert Troup, and John Laurens. It also included consequential intimate relationships, most notably the Reynolds affair, whose public disclosure damaged his reputation and affected his marriage.
